EGY_1970_shadow_of_the_naksa: Three years after the catastrophe of June 1967, Egypt is a nation at war without a victory to show for it. The Sinai lies under occupation, the Canal is shut, Soviet advisers fill the barracks and Nasser, weary and unwell, still carries the hopes of the Arab world. Every decision of the coming decade will be made in the shadow of the Naksa.
EGY_1970_mobilise_the_home_front: A country that has lost a war cannot win the next one on enthusiasm alone. The Arab Socialist Union, the trade unions and the provincial committees are called upon to keep the factories running, the fellahin loyal and the sacrifice shared. Rationing is tolerated and conscripts are fed, so long as the people believe that the burden is being borne equally.
EGY_1970_the_succession_question: Nasser's heart is failing, and everyone in Cairo knows it, though few dare say so aloud. Sadat, Sabri, Zakaria Mohieddin and the generals around Mohamed Fawzi each imagine themselves at the head of the republic. Behind the polite fiction of collective leadership, the struggle over who will inherit the Rais's authority has already begun.
EGY_1970_doctors_from_moscow: Should the best cardiologists of the Soviet Union be flown to Cairo, the Rais might yet be spared. Moscow has every reason to keep the man who anchors its position on the Nile alive, and Nasser, however reluctantly, accepts treatment and rest. The succession is postponed, though not cancelled, and the republic holds its breath with every medical bulletin.
EGY_1970_the_heir_apparent: Anwar Sadat, long dismissed as a loyal but colourless Free Officer, is named to carry the presidency after Nasser. To the generals and the party apparatus he looks like a safe transitional figure, a man to be managed rather than feared. His rivals in the Arab Socialist Union's inner circle have underestimated him, and they will come to regret it.
EGY_1970_the_centres_of_power: Should the men who built the security state refuse to be sidelined, the succession will be settled in the corridors of the Mukhabarat rather than at the ballot box. Ali Sabri and his allies move before any rival can consolidate, backed by Moscow's quiet approval. The Rais's heir is pushed aside, and the apparatus of Nasserism rules in its own name.
EGY_1970_a_cabinet_of_experts: With the old guard discredited and the army wary of open rule, a government of technocrats and elder statesmen is called to steady the ship. Zakaria Mohieddin, once named as Nasser's successor in the dark days of 1967, returns to office promising competence over ideology. Washington notices the change of tone, and so do the exhausted bureaucrats of Cairo.
EGY_1970_the_army_steps_in: When politicians quarrel over a dead man's legacy, the officers act. War Minister Mohamed Fawzi, backed by a General Staff that has little patience for party intrigue, assumes the leadership in the name of national survival. The republic remains, but it is now openly a state of soldiers, and the front along the Canal comes before everything else.
EGY_1970_the_corrective_revolution: In May 1971 Sadat moves against those who thought he would be their puppet. Ali Sabri, Sami Sharaf, Sharawi Gomaa and their colleagues are arrested, and the heart of the Nasserist security state is dismantled almost overnight. The president calls it a corrective movement, and the burning of the intelligence tapes seems to promise a freer, if still firmly governed, Egypt.
EGY_1970_a_president_in_his_own_right: However the crisis was resolved, the question of who rules Egypt has finally been answered. The new leader no longer governs in the shadow of Nasser's portrait but under his own authority, with a plebiscite to confirm what the officers and ministers have already accepted. The state can now turn from survival to direction.
EGY_1970_the_permanent_constitution: Egypt has lived under provisional constitutions since the fall of the monarchy. A permanent text is drafted to give the republic a settled legal order, defining the powers of the presidency, the role of the single party and the rights of its citizens. It is both a promise of stability and a statement of who is meant to hold the pen.
EGY_1970_sharia_as_a_principal_source: The drafters write that the principles of the Islamic sharia are a principal source of legislation. To the scholars of al-Azhar it is a vindication, to the Coptic minority a cause for unease, and to the president a useful counterweight to the left. Faith, once a matter for the mosque, is written into the foundations of the state.
EGY_1970_the_secular_charter: Egypt, the charter declares, belongs to all its citizens alike, Muslim and Copt, and its laws are made by parliament rather than by scholars. The ulema of al-Azhar protest, but the engineers, lawyers and teachers of the modern state welcome a constitution that looks forward. Religion remains honoured, though it is not to be the source of law.
EGY_1970_the_party_question: The Arab Socialist Union has been the only legal political organisation for over a decade, and it is showing its age. Some argue that unity requires a single party, others that pluralism must be allowed to breathe, and still others that the emergency must simply continue. The answer will define how Egyptians are permitted to argue with their government.
EGY_1970_one_party_one_nation: The nation is at war and cannot afford the luxury of factions. A single organisation, drawing together peasants, workers, soldiers and civil servants, is declared the only legitimate vehicle of political life. Dissent is not forbidden outright but is expected to find its voice within the Union, and nowhere else.
EGY_1970_open_the_platforms: In a bold experiment, the Arab Socialist Union is divided into platforms, or manabir, representing the left, the centre and the right. Out of these tribunes may grow genuine parties, with their own programmes and newspapers. Egypt's old liberals and leftists sense an opening, while the security services watch to see how far it will go.
EGY_1970_the_emergency_law: The state of emergency, in force since 1967, is extended and given new teeth. Suspects may be held without trial, public gatherings need permission and the press learns where the lines are drawn. The government calls it the price of facing Israel, and the men of the Mukhabarat find themselves rarely idle.
EGY_1970_egypts_place_in_the_world: The years since Suez have taught Egypt that it has friends but no certainties. Cairo must now decide whether its future lies with the neutral states of the Third World, with Moscow, with Washington, with the faith of its people or with Egypt alone. The choice made here will shape every treaty and every alliance to come.
EGY_1970_dir_positive_neutralism: Nasser's old creed of positive neutrality, forged at Bandung and Belgrade, is renewed. Egypt will take aid from whoever offers it but will serve no master, and will speak for the nations that refuse to be pawns of the great powers. It is a proud course, and a precarious one for a country at war.
EGY_1970_dir_the_socialist_camp: The Soviet Union has rebuilt Egypt's army, financed the High Dam and stationed its crews along the Canal. It seems only natural to complete the journey and to align the republic openly with the socialist camp. Planners, advisers and ideologues arrive in growing numbers, convinced that the Nile's future lies in the East.
EGY_1970_dir_the_american_card: Sadat's maxim is that ninety-nine percent of the cards in the Middle East are in American hands. Only Washington can compel Israel to withdraw from Sinai, and only Washington has the capital to lift the Egyptian economy. If Moscow's embrace has brought nothing but dependence, perhaps it is time to turn westward.
EGY_1970_dir_the_believer_state: Defeat in 1967 discredited the secular promises of the revolution, and many Egyptians now look to the mosque for answers. The idea of a state guided by faith, rather than by slogans of socialism or nationalism, grows in the lecture halls and the poorer quarters of Cairo. The leadership must decide whether to ride this current or be swept aside by it.
EGY_1970_dir_egypt_first: Egypt has bled for causes that were never entirely its own, from Yemen to Palestine to the dream of Arab unity. A new voice argues that the nation must look first to its own soil, its own interests and its own five thousand years of history. The army, which has paid the highest price for pan-Arab ambitions, listens with interest.
EGY_1970_na_voice_of_the_arabs: From its Cairo studios, Sawt al-Arab has long carried the message of the revolution to every café and village square from the Atlantic to the Gulf. Under the new leadership the broadcasts are turned to the cause of independence and non-alignment, challenging the monarchs and rallying the street. The voice of Cairo may be hoarse, but it is still heard.
EGY_1970_na_capital_of_liberation: Algerian fighters, African nationalists and exiled movements from across the Third World have long found shelter in Cairo. By opening its offices, scholarships and training camps to them, Egypt claims a role as the capital of liberation. The cost is considerable, though the prestige repays it in friends who will remember.
EGY_1970_na_the_brioni_spirit: At Brioni in 1956, Nasser, Tito and Nehru declared their refusal to join either bloc. That spirit is now revived in earnest, with Belgrade and New Delhi as natural partners in a world that wants to be neither red nor blue. Common projects, trade and diplomatic support give substance to what had been largely a slogan.
EGY_1970_na_restore_the_asu: Should the non-aligned course be entrusted to the old movement, the Arab Socialist Union is restored as the vehicle of national life. Its committees are revived and its cadres return to the villages and factories. It is the familiar face of the revolution, comfortable and well organised, if somewhat tired.
EGY_1970_na_strengthen_the_presidency: A strong presidency, above party and faction, is entrusted to a figure of experience and moderation. Zakaria Mohieddin and his circle of administrators promise efficient government without the fervour of ideology. Critics call it a technocratic monarchy, while supporters point to the order it brings.
EGY_1970_na_legalise_the_brotherhood: After years of prison camps and executions, the Muslim Brotherhood emerges into public life. Its veteran leaders, led by the aged Umar al-Tilmisani, offer a moderate programme of piety, social welfare and constitutional rule. Secular Egyptians watch with apprehension as the movement that Nasser tried to destroy takes the reins of government.
EGY_1970_na_the_independent_left: Veterans of the Free Officers who broke with the regime have kept alive a socialism that is neither Soviet nor authoritarian. Khaled Mohieddin and the National Progressive Unionist Party offer a left-wing government committed to workers' rights, civil liberties and independence from both blocs. It is a democratic experiment few thought possible.
EGY_1970_na_the_new_class: Contractors, importers and well-connected managers have grown rich under the shelter of the state. With the opening of the economy, they now seek to govern directly rather than to buy influence. The business circle of Osman Ahmed Osman promises growth and prosperity, and the poor wonder whether they will share in it.
EGY_1970_na_neither_east_nor_west: The government declares that Egypt will join no pact, host no foreign bases and bow to no capital. In the manner of Nasser's old doctrine, Cairo will seek its own path between the blocs. The words are bold, but the ministries must now find the means to make them credible.
EGY_1970_na_lead_the_nam: The Non-Aligned Movement was born in part from Egyptian initiative, and Cairo now claims its rightful place at the head of it. Summits, delegations and joint declarations carry the voice of the developing world into the councils of the great powers. A seat at the table is useful, even to a country that must still beg for spare parts.
EGY_1970_na_arms_from_all_quarters: Egypt's armoury has been Soviet for years, but a truly independent state cannot rely on a single supplier. Delegations travel to Paris, Belgrade, Beijing and beyond in search of aircraft, engines and ammunition. A diversified arsenal is harder to blackmail, if rather harder to maintain.
EGY_1970_na_let_the_blocs_compete: Moscow and Washington are each eager to claim the Nile as their own, and Cairo has learned to turn their rivalry to advantage. Every offer of credit, wheat or weapons from one is carefully shown to the other. It is a delicate and sometimes dangerous game, played with great skill by the diplomats of the Foreign Ministry.
EGY_1970_na_afro_asian_solidarity: From Addis Ababa to Dar es Salaam, newly independent states look to Cairo as an elder brother. Technical missions, teachers and trade agreements deepen the ties that were first sealed at Bandung. In the United Nations, a solid bloc of African and Asian votes will be there when Egypt needs them.
EGY_1970_na_champion_of_the_third_world: Egypt has become a spokesman for all those who resent the order imposed by Washington and Moscow alike. The republic speaks for commodity producers, former colonies and small nations demanding fair treatment. Its influence now extends far beyond what its modest wealth would suggest.
EGY_1970_na_the_notables: The old families of the provinces, the omdas and landed notables who survived the land reforms, see their moment. A cabinet drawn from their ranks promises continuity, respect for property and a government that knows the countryside. Reformers warn that the Egypt of Nasser is being quietly unwound.
EGY_1970_na_the_free_economy: Free-market economists and importers argue that the Egyptian economy has been strangled by state control. A government committed to liberalisation promises to dismantle subsidies, open the markets and let private enterprise lead. The bazaar cheers, though the factory floors are anxious.
EGY_1970_na_the_friends_of_the_nile: A new kind of politics emerges around the great river itself. Ecologists, agronomists and engineers warn of the silt held back by the High Dam, the salt creeping into the Delta and the fouling of the Nile. They ask Egypt to measure its progress not by tonnes of steel but by the health of the river that gave it life.
EGY_1970_em_scientific_socialism: Nasser's Arab socialism was always more instinct than doctrine. Now the ideologues of the Socialist Union argue for something firmer, a scientific socialism taught in the party schools and applied through the plan. Marxist economists, long tolerated on the margins, find themselves invited to the centre of policy.
EGY_1970_em_advisers_in_every_ministry: Soviet specialists already train the army and run the missile batteries on the Canal. Now they are welcomed into the planning offices, the factories and the ministries themselves. Their guidance is invaluable, though some Egyptians mutter that they sit at the desk of every minister.
EGY_1970_em_the_vanguard_organisation: Inside the Arab Socialist Union, a secret cadre known as the Vanguard Organisation has been quietly recruited from the most committed and trusted militants. Formalised and expanded, it becomes the disciplined core of the revolution, shaping policy from behind the scenes. Loyalty to the cause is rewarded, and doubt is noticed.
EGY_1970_em_power_to_the_vanguard: Ali Sabri and the Vanguard cadres take command of the state in their own name. The apparatus built over a decade, from the intelligence service to the party committees, is now unmistakably the government. Moscow nods with approval, and the more independent minds of the revolution fall silent.
EGY_1970_em_power_to_the_communists: The Egyptian communists dissolved their party in 1965 to join Nasser's Union, and have long worked within the system. Now their moment appears to have come, as veteran cadres emerge from the prison camps and the underground to claim the leadership. The red flag is raised over a country that has never been ruled by one.
EGY_1970_em_power_to_the_councils: From the textile mills of Mahalla to the shipyards of Alexandria, workers declare that the revolution belongs to them rather than to the officials who speak for them. Councils elected on the factory floor seize the means of production and form the basis of a new government. It is a socialism from below, deeply unsettling to every established authority.
EGY_1970_em_power_to_the_misr_party: Fearing the chaos of revolution, a coalition of officers, landowners and conservative bureaucrats installs a government of order. They promise to protect property, restrain the radicals and keep the Soviet advisers on a short leash. The language is still that of progress, though the spirit is one of caution.
EGY_1970_em_power_to_the_islamic_front: A radical vision takes hold, in which the revolution is not socialist but Islamic, aimed at the overthrow of both the corrupt state and its foreign patrons. Inspired by events far beyond the Nile, activists and clerics rally to a new front. Their government makes the faith, rather than the plan, the engine of the revolution.
EGY_1970_em_power_to_the_guardians: A clerical leadership seizes the state in the name of the revolution, claiming that sovereignty belongs to the guardianship of the jurist rather than to the people or the party. The officers resist and the Azhar scholars are divided, but the new rulers are convinced that they carry a divine mandate. Egypt becomes a very different kind of republic.
EGY_1970_em_the_progressive_front: All the forces of the left, from Nasserist cadres to Marxist intellectuals and trade unionists, are gathered into a single Progressive National Front. Old disputes are set aside in the name of unity against reaction and imperialism. The Front is meant to be a broad coalition, though its leadership is firmly in the hands of the committed.
EGY_1970_em_the_state_planning_committee: A powerful planning committee is empowered to direct industry, agriculture and trade in accordance with the needs of the nation. Five-year plans are drafted with Soviet help, targets are set for steel, cotton and power, and the market is relegated to the margins. Efficiency is hoped for, though bureaucracy is feared.
EGY_1970_em_comecon_partnership: The trade of Egypt, long dominated by the purchase of cotton by the Eastern bloc, is brought into closer cooperation with the economies of Comecon. Moscow and its allies offer credits, machinery and technical expertise in exchange for lasting economic ties. The Nile valley is drawn further into a planned economic community.
EGY_1970_em_peoples_militias: Armed workers' and peasants' militias are raised in the factories and villages, drilled by army instructors and commanded by party loyalists. They guard the Canal towns, watch the streets and remind the regular army that the revolution has its own defenders. For many Egyptians it is the first time they have held a rifle.
EGY_1970_em_join_the_socialist_camp: Egypt formally takes its place among the nations of the socialist camp. The long courtship with the East ends in an alliance, with all the obligations it carries. Cairo is now a pillar of the anti-imperialist front, rather than a wary guest.
EGY_1970_em_red_star_over_the_nile: The transformation is complete. From the Aswan Dam to the Delta, posters, plans and slogans proclaim a socialist Egypt, building a new society with the friendship of the socialist world. The pyramids look down on a very different kind of republic, and the Rais would hardly recognise it.
EGY_1970_we_99_percent_of_the_cards: Sadat's famous remark, that ninety-nine percent of the cards in the Middle East are held by America, becomes the guiding principle of foreign policy. Only through Washington can Egypt hope to recover Sinai peacefully and revive its economy. Cairo opens its channels to the State Department, and American diplomats begin to visit more often.
EGY_1970_we_the_investment_law: Law 43 invites foreign and Arab capital to Egypt on generous terms, with tax holidays, guarantees against nationalisation and freedom to repatriate profits. The architects of the Open Door hope for factories, hotels and banks. The trade unions, who built the public sector, fear what will become of their jobs.
EGY_1970_we_lift_the_censorship: The censors who once sat in every newsroom are withdrawn, and Egyptian writers speak openly for the first time in years. Newspapers criticise ministers, satirists mock the establishment and political prisoners are quietly released. The government hopes that candour will win loyalty, though it also unleashes a flood of grievances.
EGY_1970_we_power_to_the_ndp: The president forms a new ruling party, drawn from the centre of the old Arab Socialist Union and open to businessmen, officials and the rural elite. Disciplined and pragmatic, it is meant to guide the Open Door without losing control of the state. It is a party of government rather than of ideas.
EGY_1970_we_power_to_the_wafd: The Wafd, the great nationalist party of Saad Zaghloul and Nahhas Pasha, returns from its long exile. Its elderly leaders, led by Fouad Serageddin, offer a government of liberal constitutionalism, free markets and respect for the law. For some it is a restoration, for others a reminder of the corrupt politics that the officers once overthrew.
EGY_1970_we_power_to_the_liberals: A cabinet of liberals comes to office, committed to economic freedom, the rule of law and a prudent foreign policy. Their programme is modest and their ministers experienced, with little patience for slogans. They promise an Egypt governed by reason, not by revolutionary fervour.
EGY_1970_we_power_to_socialist_labour: Socialist Labour, a loyal opposition drawn from the old left of the Union, forms a government that embraces the West without abandoning the working class. It promises a welfare state, trade union rights and a social market economy. Its leaders hope to prove that openness need not mean inequality.
EGY_1970_we_the_open_door: The Open Door, or Infitah, is proclaimed, and the economy is turned towards private enterprise and foreign capital. The sealed system of Nasserism gives way to imported goods, joint ventures and new fortunes along the Nile. Egyptians will be richer in some respects and more divided in others.
EGY_1970_we_the_usaid_mission: American aid officials open offices in Cairo for the first time in years. Wheat shipments, development loans and technical missions begin to flow along the diplomatic channel, proof of what friendship with Washington may bring. Egyptians ask what price will eventually be named.
EGY_1970_we_the_imf_standby: To rescue the treasury, Egypt turns to the International Monetary Fund, which offers help on condition that the government cut its subsidies on bread, rice and cooking oil. The economists call it necessary medicine, and the poor of Cairo call it theft. The streets will deliver their own verdict.
EGY_1970_we_step_by_step_diplomacy: Rather than seek a single grand settlement, Egypt entrusts itself to Henry Kissinger's patient diplomacy, in which small withdrawals build confidence for larger ones. The shuttle flights between Aswan, Jerusalem and Damascus become the pulse of regional politics. Each step is modest, but together they might lead somewhere.
EGY_1970_we_join_the_free_world: Egypt formally takes its place beside the Western democracies. Its markets, its diplomacy and its armed forces are increasingly woven into the Atlantic order, and the slogans of non-alignment give way to the language of partnership. After two decades of confrontation with the West, Cairo has chosen its side.
EGY_1970_we_americas_partner: Washington comes to regard Egypt as the keystone of its policy in the Middle East. Military cooperation, joint exercises and steady financial support follow, reinforced by the personal confidence between the two presidents. The most populous Arab state has become a pillar of the American order.
EGY_1970_sa_the_gamaat_on_campus: In the universities of Cairo, Assiut and Minya, Islamic student groups are encouraged to challenge the Marxists and Nasserists who dominate campus life. Backed by the authorities, they win student elections and set new standards of dress and conduct. The movement they build will outgrow its sponsors.
EGY_1970_sa_petrodollar_piety: Egyptian teachers, engineers and labourers travel to the Gulf, and return with money, conservative habits and a stricter piety. Saudi donors fund mosques, charities and religious schools along the Nile. Faith and finance have become inseparable partners in the shaping of public life.
EGY_1970_sa_the_hisba: The ancient institution of the hisba, by which the community enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong, is revived. Inspectors move through the markets and streets, watching weights, dress and public morals. Supporters see a return to virtue, while others see a licence for self-appointed guardians.
EGY_1970_sa_power_to_the_azhar: The scholars of al-Azhar, guardians of Sunni learning for a thousand years, are called to govern. The Grand Imam Abd al-Halim Mahmud brings moderation, scholarship and the weight of tradition to the highest office of the state. The mosque and the ministry become one in a more orderly fashion than many feared.
EGY_1970_sa_power_to_the_jamaat: The young militants of the Jama'at, radicalised on campus and hardened in prison, decide that the existing order is beyond reform. Their uprising overthrows the old establishment and installs an Emir in the capital. The army is shaken, the streets are tense, and the revolution devours its elders.
EGY_1970_sa_the_islamic_order: Egypt is proclaimed an Islamic state, and the constitution, courts and schools are to be reshaped accordingly. The government presents the change as a return to the true foundations of the nation, and a repudiation of the failures of secular nationalism. A new republic begins, bound to the law of God.
EGY_1970_sa_zakat_instead_of_taxes: The religious duty of zakat is made the basis of public welfare, collected in the mosques and distributed to the poor. The state trusts charity and conscience to do what the planners of the socialist era could not. Many welcome the dignity of giving, though the treasury wonders how it will pay for roads and schools.
EGY_1970_sa_islamic_economics: The banks of Egypt are reorganised on Islamic principles, with interest forbidden and profit shared between investor and borrower. Economists debate whether a modern economy can function in this way, while the devout watch with hope. It is an experiment on a national scale.
EGY_1970_sa_the_pan_islamic_turn: The new Egypt looks beyond the Arab world to the wider community of believers. Riyadh, Islamabad and Khartoum receive delegations from Cairo, and the old rhetoric of Arab nationalism is replaced by that of Muslim brotherhood. The ummah, not the nation, becomes the horizon of Egyptian diplomacy.
EGY_1970_sa_al_quds_first: The liberation of Jerusalem is proclaimed a duty of every Muslim, not merely of the Arabs. Sermons, camps and recruiting posters call the faithful to the defence of the third holiest city of Islam. Israel is no longer merely an enemy of the state but of the faith.
EGY_1970_sa_dar_al_islam: The transformation of Egyptian society is now far advanced. Law, education, commerce and the family are ordered by the principles of the faith, and the state sees itself as the keeper of a house of Islam on the Nile. For better or worse, the old republic is gone.
EGY_1970_nt_faith_in_the_army: In the shadow of defeat, the army remains the one institution that Egyptians still believe can redeem the nation. Its officers, drawn from the villages and small towns, are held up as the embodiment of the people's will. Trust in the uniform is restored, and with it, expectations of those who wear it.
EGY_1970_nt_pharaonic_heritage: Egypt is older than Islam, older than the Arabs and older than any of the nations that have lectured it on unity. Historians, artists and schoolbooks celebrate the Pharaohs as the nation's ancestors, and the monuments of Giza as its birthright. Arab brethren look on with unease at this reorientation of identity.
EGY_1970_nt_the_officers_clubs: The officers' clubs of Cairo and Alexandria have long been places for meals, sport and conversation. Now they become the meeting places of a political class, where careers are made and plans are quietly drawn. The army is no longer merely a servant of the republic but its natural guardian.
EGY_1970_nt_power_to_the_army: Field Marshals and Chiefs of Staff assume the government of Egypt in the name of the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces. Generals such as Saad el-Shazly and Mohamed Fawzi bring discipline, planning and a deep suspicion of civilian politicians. The republic is secure in their hands, though few are certain when they will give it back.
EGY_1970_nt_power_to_young_egypt: The old Misr al-Fatat, once the green-shirted youth movement of Egyptian nationalism, rises from obscurity. Its leaders promise discipline, honour and a rebirth of the nation under a populist banner. The Nile's youth respond to the call, and the old establishment looks on in alarm.
EGY_1970_nt_power_to_the_rcc: Young colonels, impatient with their senior officers and with the failures of the revolution, form a new Revolutionary Command Council. They denounce corruption and compromise, and promise a harder, purer nationalism. The memory of 1952 hangs over them, for they intend to do it all again.
EGY_1970_nt_restore_the_crown: A surprising turn in the officers' councils brings the question of the monarchy back into the open. Fuad II, the infant king deposed in 1952, is invoked as a symbol of continuity above faction and politics. For some the throne is a relic, for others the only legitimate answer to a generation of revolutionary turmoil.
EGY_1970_nt_the_officers_republic: The republic of the officers is openly declared, and the armed forces take the lead in public life. Governors, ministers and company directors are drawn from the ranks, and the logic of the barracks spreads through the state. Order and duty are the watchwords of the new Egypt.
EGY_1970_nt_martial_law: Martial law is declared, and the military courts, patrols and curfews give the authorities the power to act without delay. Strikes are broken, demonstrations dispersed and troublemakers detained. The streets are calm, at least on the surface.
EGY_1970_nt_the_war_economy: Egypt reorganises its economy for a long struggle. Factories are turned to military production, consumer goods are rationed, and civilian planning is subordinated to the needs of the army. It is a lean and austere regime, but it keeps the guns supplied.
EGY_1970_nt_the_national_service_project: The army builds its own economic empire. The National Service Projects Organisation takes on the production of everything from bottled water to pasta, using conscript labour and military engineers to supply the state. The generals have discovered that a nation's defence rests as much on its factories as on its tanks.
EGY_1970_nt_egypt_above_all: Egypt above all, say the posters, the speeches and the schoolbooks. Loyalty to the nation is placed before party, class and creed, and the citizen is asked to accept sacrifice for the sake of the whole. It is a stern gospel, but one that a proud and bruised country is ready to hear.
EGY_1970_nt_a_nation_in_arms: From the schoolchild to the reservist, the whole population is drawn into the national defence. Military training, civil defence drills and the glorification of service become part of daily life. Egypt has become a nation in arms, with its army at the centre.
EGY_1970_the_war_of_attrition: Since 1968 the guns along the Suez Canal have never been fully silent. Artillery duels, air raids and commando strikes bleed both sides while the Bar-Lev Line stands defiantly on the far bank. Nasser calls it a war of attrition, convinced that Egypt's greater numbers and patience will eventually wear Israel down.
EGY_1970_the_missile_wall: As Israeli aircraft strike deep into the Nile Valley, the answer is a belt of surface-to-air missile batteries, rolled forward towards the Canal with Soviet crews and Egyptian sweat. Under their umbrella, the army can at last work without fear from the sky. It is the shield that makes any future crossing possible.
EGY_1970_commandos_across_the_canal: Small parties of Egyptian commandos slip across the Canal at night to ambush patrols, mine roads and strike at the outposts of the Bar-Lev Line. The raids achieve little in terms of ground, but they restore the confidence of an army that has known only retreat. Each returning boat is a small victory over the memory of 1967.
EGY_1970_the_rogers_plan: Washington's Secretary of State proposes a ceasefire along the Canal, and a framework for talks under Ambassador Jarring. The offer is fraught with risk, for it offers a pause while Israel remains in Sinai. Egypt must weigh the relief of the cities against the dangers of letting the moment pass.
EGY_1970_accept_the_ceasefire: Egypt accepts the proposal and the guns fall silent along the Canal. The cities of Suez and Ismailia breathe at last, and the missile batteries creep forward under the cover of calm. Hardliners call it surrender, but the president insists it is a pause for breath, not an end to the struggle.
EGY_1970_no_peace_without_sinai: There will be no ceasefire, no negotiation and no recognition while Israeli soldiers stand on Egyptian soil. The Rogers Plan is rejected as a trap that would freeze the occupation, and the war of attrition continues. Cairo has made its choice, and the cost will be paid by its soldiers.
EGY_1970_operation_granite_plan: In the offices of the General Staff, planners draw up Granite, a full-scale scheme to cross the Canal, storm the Bar-Lev Line and penetrate deep into Sinai. Ambitious and detailed, it is a plan of the kind that Egypt could not yet carry out. The work, however, builds a habit of thinking that will serve it well.
EGY_1970_the_high_minarets: Chief of Staff Saad el-Shazly argues that Egypt should not outreach its means. A more limited plan, called the High Minarets, would cross the Canal and seize a narrow strip on the far side, remaining under the protection of the missile umbrella. It is a prudent strategy of an army that has learned humility the hard way.
EGY_1970_water_cannons_against_sand: The great sand rampart of the Bar-Lev Line seems to defy the engineers, until a young officer suggests that high-pressure water pumps could wash it away. The idea is tested on sandbanks along the Nile, and the results are startling. A problem measured in days of labour is solved in hours.
EGY_1970_the_great_deception: Year after year the army stages exercises at the Canal, each of which ends in a stand-down. Israeli intelligence grows accustomed to the pattern, and the reports from the front begin to say that nothing is happening. By the time a real attack comes, nobody believes in it.
EGY_1970_operation_badr: The plans are complete, the units are in place and the men are trained to the last detail. Operation Badr, named for the Prophet's first great victory, awaits only the order. When it comes, it will be the culmination of six years of preparation and a lifetime of humiliation.
EGY_1970_the_crossing: On a clear afternoon the Egyptian army surges across the Canal, bursting the Bar-Lev Line and raising the flag on the eastern bank. The shock to Israel is profound, and the pride of Egypt is restored. The defeat of 1967, which weighed upon a generation, is lifted at last.
EGY_1970_coordinate_the_oil_weapon: Egypt cannot compel the oil producers to act, but it can ask. Envoys travel to Riyadh, Tripoli, Baghdad and Kuwait to urge them to use their wealth as a weapon against the states that arm Israel. The decision is theirs alone, and Cairo awaits their answer.
EGY_1970_kilometre_101: At a tent beside the Cairo-Suez road, Egyptian and Israeli officers meet to discuss the exchange of prisoners and the future of the front. It is the first face-to-face encounter between the two armies, and the beginning of a more serious dialogue. The road to disengagement starts at Kilometre 101.
EGY_1970_the_sinai_agreement: After years of tense negotiation, Cairo and Jerusalem are asked to agree on the phased return of Sinai, in exchange for demilitarised zones and international monitors. The terms are bitter to some and generous to others, but they promise the return of every grain of Egyptian sand. Peace is no longer an abstraction.
EGY_1970_reopen_the_suez_canal: Eight years of silence end when engineers and naval divers clear the wrecks and mines that choke the waterway. Ships once again pass between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, and the revenues of the Canal return to the Egyptian treasury. The great artery of world trade flows once more through the heart of Egypt.
EGY_1970_rebuild_the_canal_cities: Suez, Ismailia and Port Said, evacuated and shelled for years, are left in ruins. Now their inhabitants return to rebuild their homes, their harbours and their workshops. The new cities rise from the rubble with great hope, and a certain pride in having survived.
EGY_1970_honour_regained: The sixth of October becomes a national holiday, a day on which Egyptians remember the crossing and the soldiers who made it possible. The shame of the Naksa has been erased, not by the extent of victory but by the proof of courage. The army, and the nation, can hold their heads high again.
EGY_1970_leader_of_the_arab_world: Cairo has always seen itself as the natural capital of the Arab world, and Nasser as its leader. Even after the defeat, its schools, its broadcasts and its diplomats continue to shape the Arab debate. The mantle of leadership is heavy, but Egypt is not ready to lay it down.
EGY_1970_mediate_black_september: In the autumn of 1970, Jordan's army and the Palestinian fedayeen are locked in a bloody struggle. Nasser, exhausted but still the only figure trusted by both sides, convenes an emergency summit in Cairo. His last act of statesmanship is to bring King Hussein and Yasser Arafat to the same table.
EGY_1970_the_khartoum_subsidies: At Khartoum in 1967, the oil-rich monarchies pledged annual aid to the Arab states that bore the brunt of the war. The money is vital to an economy strained by military spending and the loss of Canal revenue. Egypt keeps its patrons reassured that their generosity serves the common cause.
EGY_1970_the_tripoli_charter: Colonel Gaddafi, young, zealous and admiring of Nasser, offers Libya's wealth and his own devotion to the cause of Arab unity. Together with Sudan's new rulers, Egypt signs a charter of cooperation at Tripoli. It is a bold gesture towards a union that many have dreamed of and none have achieved.
EGY_1970_federation_of_arab_republics: Egypt, Libya and Syria announce the formation of a Federation of Arab Republics, with a shared presidential council and common aspirations. The ceremony is grand, the speeches are long and the declarations are heartfelt. Whether the federation will be more than a name remains to be seen.
EGY_1970_full_union_with_libya: Gaddafi insists that unity must be real, not merely symbolic, and calls for a full merger of Egypt and Libya. Marches of Libyan supporters head towards Cairo, and the oil wealth of the desert is dangled before the Nile. The proposal tempts some in Egypt and alarms many others.
EGY_1970_a_loose_federation: Egypt prefers a loose association of sovereign states, with limited powers and few obligations. The enthusiasm of Tripoli cools, and the fervour of the unionists is disappointed. For Cairo, prudence is the better part of brotherhood.
EGY_1970_unity_of_the_nile_valley: Egypt and Sudan are bound together by the river, by history and by blood. Talk of a joint economic union, with common markets, shared agricultural projects and the integration of the Nile valley, revives an old dream. The brothers of the Nile look to a future in which Khartoum and Cairo face the world as one.
EGY_1970_the_uar_reborn: The dream of 1958 is born anew. Egypt, Syria and their partners proclaim the rebirth of the United Arab Republic, a union forged by the experience of failure rather than naive enthusiasm. A flag with three stars rises again, and the Arab world watches with hope and apprehension.
EGY_1970_host_the_plo: Cairo offers a home to the Palestine Liberation Organisation, with offices, broadcasts and recognition as the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people. Arafat's fighters find a patron who shares their cause, if not always their methods. Israel notes the welcome and draws its own conclusions.
EGY_1970_the_arab_league_in_cairo: The Arab League, whose headquarters have long been in Cairo, becomes an instrument of Egyptian diplomacy. Summits, committees and resolutions are shaped in the corridors of Tahrir. The Arab world speaks, as it often does, with a Cairene accent.
EGY_1970_arab_industrialisation_organisa: Egyptian engineering, Saudi and Emirati money and Western technology are joined in a great enterprise to build an independent Arab arms industry. Factories rise near Cairo to produce missiles, aircraft and vehicles, freeing the Arab world from the whims of foreign suppliers. The project is costly, but the prize is independence.
EGY_1970_workers_to_the_gulf: Teachers, doctors, clerks and construction workers leave the overcrowded Nile valley to seek their fortunes in the Gulf. The remittances they send home feed families, support the currency and ease unemployment. The country gains money, though it loses many of its best-trained sons.
EGY_1970_between_moscow_and_washington: Egypt stands between two giants, dependent on one for weapons and courted by the other for peace. Every decision, from the purchase of a rifle to the drafting of a communique, is weighed against the reaction in two capitals. Cairo's diplomats must walk a narrow path between them.
EGY_1970_operation_kavkaz: As Israeli deep-penetration raids humiliate Egyptian air defences, Nasser flies secretly to Moscow to beg for more help. The Kremlin responds by sending Soviet missile crews and fighter pilots, a deployment of astonishing scale and secrecy. For a time, Russians guard the skies above the Nile.
EGY_1970_the_moscow_anchor: Egypt anchors its security to Moscow, accepting advisers, missiles and tanks in exchange for political loyalty. The dependence is considerable, but the arsenals of the Soviet Union are formidable and its support has never wavered. The Kremlin's friendship is a refuge as well as a leash.
EGY_1970_the_washington_channel: A secret line opens between Cairo and Washington, carrying messages from Hafez Ismail to Henry Kissinger. The two sides test each other's intentions and explore the possibilities of peace. Moscow, naturally, would not be pleased.
EGY_1970_positive_neutrality: Egypt declines to be the property of either power. It accepts the wheat and the weapons of both blocs while committing itself to neither, and presents itself as the champion of independent states everywhere. The balance is delicate, and a stumble might cost dearly.
EGY_1970_treaty_of_friendship: In May 1971 Egypt and the Soviet Union sign a treaty of friendship and cooperation, binding the two states in a formal alliance. Moscow promises continued support in the face of Israeli aggression, and Cairo pledges its steadfastness to the common cause. For a decade, it will be the cornerstone of the Egyptian military posture.
EGY_1970_scuds_and_sam_6: With the treaty signed, Soviet industry opens its arsenal. Mobile SAM-6 batteries with their radars, SCUD missiles with their promise of long reach and the technical missions that accompany them appear along the Nile. Egyptian crews learn their craft with unusual speed.
EGY_1970_join_the_soviet_bloc: Egypt takes its place within the Soviet sphere, with all that it implies. Its armies, its industries and its diplomacy are tied to the Eastern bloc. The Kremlin welcomes a new ally, the largest in the Arab world.
EGY_1970_expel_the_soviet_advisers: In July 1972 the Soviet advisers are given a week to leave. Sadat reasons that Moscow offers too little and demands too much, and that Egypt cannot negotiate with Washington while Russian experts fill its barracks. The protection of the missile umbrella vanishes with them, which is a bold gamble.
EGY_1970_kissingers_shuttle: The American Secretary of State shuttles tirelessly between Cairo, Jerusalem and Damascus, carrying proposals, assurances and warnings. Each journey brings the parties a little closer. Egyptian diplomats, once strangers to Washington, find themselves leading the conversation.
EGY_1970_join_the_western_bloc: Egypt completes its reorientation by joining the Western camp. Its former reliance on Moscow is replaced by cooperation with Washington and its allies. The change is sweeping, and few of the old comrades are left to mourn it.
EGY_1970_mig_engines_from_beijing: With the Soviet Union estranged, the Egyptian air force faces a shortage of engines for its MiG fighters. China, which has its own quarrel with Moscow, offers replacement parts without any political demands. It is a modest but timely friendship.
EGY_1970_mirages_from_paris: France, the one Western power that has not forgotten its older ties to the Arab world, is willing to sell fighters and electronics where others will not. Egyptian pilots look at the Mirage with interest. De Gaulle's heirs find in Cairo a customer with deep pockets.
EGY_1970_pivot_of_the_cold_war: In the cold war's long contest for the Middle East, no state counts for more than Egypt. Its choice of ally has changed the balance of the region, and both camps know it. Whoever holds the Nile holds the key to the East.
